title: Mara and the Typewriter
premise: In the aftermath of a civil war, Bram Joubert has survived three years as a battlefield nurse by keeping two ledgers: one for the victors, and one, typed on a smuggled typewriter, recording the names of the dead that officers deliberately omit. When a census taker's probing questions expose her to suspicion, Bram realizes the port authorities will seal the records—and her own fate—within days. Racing against a ship sailing on the morning tide, she must smuggle her true ledger into the hands of a departing historian before the victors' version of events becomes the only one. She succeeds at the cost of her anonymity, choosing exile over silence, but knowing the names are finally on the record.
about_author: Beatrix Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing war correspondence in coastal municipal libraries. She writes historical fiction about the people history forgot to count.

chapters.title: The Second Ledger
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. In a requisitioned hospital near the harbor, Bram tends the wounded by day and types the omitted names of the dead by night, hiding the true ledger beneath a floorboard. A routine census taker arrives and asks why a woman with no registered surname holds medical authority. Emotional beat: the quiet dread of a carefully built invisibility beginning to crack.

chapters.title: One Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, with an interlude from census taker Ilse Vann's perspective. Ilse returns with pointed questions about a massacre Bram's own reports helped sanitize; meanwhile officers announce all port records will be sealed and shipped for the official history. Bram learns Ilse suspects her but may not be loyal to the regime. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into resolve—silence is no longer survivable.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The night before the ship sails, Bram retrieves the ledger, evades a curfew patrol, and confronts Ilse, who must choose between reporting her and helping her. In the climax, Bram slips aboard the transport carrying the historians' crates and hides her typed pages among them, nearly caught by the officer whose omissions she documented. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into defiance.

chapters.title: What the Record Keeps
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV, then Bram's. The ship departs with the truth aboard; Ilse files a report naming Bram as a nurse of unregistered status but omits the ledger, her small act of loyalty to memory. Bram burns her spare pages, registers under a new name, and takes work inland, free and erased at once. Final beat: bittersweet resolution—the price of survival paid, the names preserved beyond her reach.
